questions.stem: A client presents with fever, abrupt severe headache, photophobia, and nuchal rigidity. A family member reports the client was well yesterday. Which condition should the nurse prioritize as the most likely explanation?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Meningitis, because fever with severe headache, photophobia, and neck stiffness is a classic meningeal symptom cluster that requires urgent evaluation.","B":"Subarachnoid hemorrhage, because abrupt severe headache and meningeal irritation can cause photophobia and neck stiffness even without an infectious cause.","C":"Migraine with aura, because severe headache and photophobia can be prominent while neck discomfort may occur from guarding during a prolonged attack.","D":"Systemic viral illness with tension-type headache, because fever and headache can coexist and produce generalized muscle stiffness during acute infection."}}
questions.rationale: CDC identifies fever, headache, and stiff neck as common features of meningococcal meningitis, and photophobia can accompany meningitis; prompt diagnosis and treatment are important. Option A therefore best matches the complete infectious meningeal cluster. Option B can cause abrupt severe headache and meningeal irritation but does not as well explain the fever in this presentation. Option C can cause headache and photophobia but does not account well for fever with true nuchal rigidity. Option D may cause fever and generalized aches but does not adequately explain this combination of severe headache, photophobia, and nuchal rigidity.
questions.source_detail: CDC's About Meningitis page, updated September 9, 2025, lists fever, headache, stiff neck, and photophobia among common meningitis symptoms and advises immediate medical evaluation; currentness was rechecked against CDC's June 4, 2026 meningococcal clinical guidance.

questions.stem: A teenage client presents with sudden severe unilateral scrotal pain, nausea, and vomiting. Testicular torsion is strongly suspected. Which action is most appropriate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Obtain Doppler ultrasonography first and contact urology after imaging if torsion remains likely, because imaging can help distinguish causes of acute scrotal pain.","B":"Arrange immediate urologic evaluation for suspected testicular torsion, because prompt detorsion is critical and is ideally completed within 4–6 hours of pain onset.","C":"Begin empiric treatment for epididymitis while awaiting outpatient reassessment, because infection can also cause unilateral scrotal pain and tenderness in adolescents.","D":"Attempt manual detorsion and observe the response before arranging surgery, because symptom improvement can help determine whether operative exploration is needed."}}
questions.rationale: The EAU guideline identifies testicular torsion as a pediatric urologic emergency requiring immediate treatment and notes a critical 4–6-hour window; option B is therefore best. Option A is inferior because Doppler ultrasound is useful but should not delay intervention when torsion is suspected. Option C risks a dangerous delay by treating presumed epididymitis without first resolving the torsion emergency. Option D is unsafe because manual detorsion may be attempted while awaiting surgery but symptom relief does not replace urgent surgical exploration and fixation.
questions.source_name: European Association of Urology — Paediatric Urology Guideline: Acute Scrotum
questions.source_detail: Current EAU guidance states that sudden severe scrotal pain with nausea/vomiting is typical of torsion, the critical window is approximately 4–6 hours, Doppler ultrasound should not delay intervention, and urgent surgical exploration is required.

questions.stem: A client with benign prostatic hyperplasia has severe lower abdominal discomfort, has been unable to void for several hours, and has a palpable distended bladder. Which condition and response are most appropriate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Acute cystitis with secondary voiding difficulty, managed first with urine studies and antimicrobial treatment while monitoring the bladder distention.","B":"Renal colic from ureteral obstruction, managed first with analgesia and imaging because severe urinary tract pain can temporarily interfere with voiding.","C":"Acute urinary retention from bladder outlet obstruction, requiring prompt bladder decompression with catheterization while the underlying cause is evaluated.","D":"Chronic urinary retention related to BPH, managed initially with outpatient medication adjustment because a palpable bladder can occur without urgent decompression."}}
questions.rationale: Merck/MSD describes acute urinary retention as cessation of urination, commonly from outlet obstruction in men, and states that relief requires urethral catheterization; BPH can cause sudden complete retention with abdominal discomfort and bladder distention. Option C therefore best fits. Option A does not explain the full distended-bladder retention syndrome and delaying decompression for antibiotics would be inappropriate. Option B describes upper-tract obstruction and does not best account for a palpable distended bladder with complete inability to void. Option D misclassifies an acute painful inability to void as chronic retention and delays required decompression.
questions.source_name: Merck/MSD Manual Professional Edition — Urinary Retention
questions.source_detail: Full review March 2026, updated April 2026. The manual describes acute and chronic urinary retention, notes prostate abnormalities as a common cause of outlet obstruction in men, and states that relief of acute urinary retention requires urethral catheterization.

questions.stem: A client develops a severe systemic allergic-like reaction immediately after iodinated IV contrast. An IgE-mediated mechanism has not been established. Which principle should guide emergency treatment?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Begin antihistamine and corticosteroid therapy while monitoring closely, and reserve epinephrine until additional findings clarify whether the reaction is IgE mediated.","B":"Manage the event as a physiologic contrast reaction with oxygen and IV fluids because lack of prior sensitization makes a severe allergic-like mechanism less likely.","C":"Stop the contrast and observe the initial response before escalating therapy, because many contrast reactions improve after exposure ends and supportive care begins.","D":"Treat the reaction according to its allergic-like severity, using epinephrine promptly when indicated for severe airway, bronchospastic, or hypotensive manifestations."}}
questions.rationale: The 2026 ACR Manual explains that most immediate allergic-like contrast reactions are not typical IgE-mediated reactions and that prior sensitization is not required; its adult treatment tables use epinephrine for severe bronchospasm, laryngeal edema, and persistent hypotensive allergic-like reactions. Option D therefore best reflects emergency management. Option A inappropriately delays epinephrine for mechanistic confirmation, and corticosteroids are not useful for acute treatment. Option B incorrectly reclassifies a severe allergic-like presentation as physiologic. Option C risks delaying indicated emergency therapy while waiting to see whether the reaction resolves.
questions.source_name: American College of Radiology — Manual on Contrast Media 2026
questions.source_detail: ACR Manual on Contrast Media 2026 states that most immediate allergic-like reactions are not typical IgE-mediated reactions, prior sensitization is not required, and adult treatment tables include epinephrine for severe bronchospasm, laryngeal edema, and persistent hypotensive allergic-like reactions.

questions.stem: A nurse is interpreting the baseline fetal heart rate during labor. Which baseline range is considered normal in the standardized three-tier intrapartum interpretation system?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"90–110 beats/min, a range that can be accepted as a normal baseline when variability is moderate and no recurrent decelerations are present.","B":"100–170 beats/min, a range that represents the normal baseline used by the current three-tier intrapartum classification system.","C":"120–180 beats/min, a range that remains within normal limits unless persistent fetal tachycardia develops with additional tracing abnormalities.","D":"110–160 beats/min, the normal baseline range used in the current standardized intrapartum fetal heart-rate classification system."}}
questions.rationale: ACOG standardized intrapartum terminology defines a normal fetal heart-rate baseline as 110–160 beats/min, making option D correct. Option A includes values below the bradycardia threshold. Option B widens both the lower and upper limits beyond the standard range. Option C excludes normal values from 110–119 and includes values above the tachycardia threshold. ACOG's October 2025 Clinical Practice Guideline No. 10 continues to use the three-tier intrapartum classification framework, so the item was currentness-checked against the newer guideline.
questions.source_name: ACOG — Standardized Fetal Heart Tracing Definitions; currentness checked against CPG No. 10 (October 2025)
questions.source_detail: ACOG's fetal heart tracing definitions list a normal baseline of 110–160 beats/min and use the three-tier system. Currentness was independently checked against ACOG Clinical Practice Guideline No. 10, Intrapartum Fetal Heart Rate Monitoring: Interpretation and Management (October 2025).
